title: One small mercy
hookLine: on a bad day, look for one small mercy

lines: A LINE IN A BOOK OF GRIEF.
cards: The alarm didn't go off. The train sat in a tunnel, going nowhere. There was a hard email before lunch, and a call from the clinic that ended with, we'll need to run more tests.
Then, on the walk home, a stranger held the door at the corner shop, and there was one of the good rolls left, still warm. Small. Nearly nothing.
It didn't fix the day. But it was there. An old book of grief has a line about exactly that, set right in the middle of its sorrow.

teach.h: A BOOK OF POEMS OVER RUINS.
teach.b: First, where the line lives. Lamentations is a book of poems over a ruined city. It is full of anguish.
In the third chapter the poet says, "thou hast removed my soul far off from peace: I forgat prosperity." He has forgotten what good even feels like. Second, the turn.
A few verses later, nothing outside has changed. The city is still in ruins.

teach.h: THIS I RECALL TO MY MIND.
teach.b: But he writes, "This I recall to my mind, therefore have I hope." And then: "It is of the LORD's mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not. They are new every morning." Notice the verb.
He recalls. He doesn't deny the ruins; he turns his attention, on purpose, to something else that is also true. Third, the word.
The Hebrew behind mercies is hesed.
English Bibles translate it in different ways: mercy, kindness, lovingkindness. Jews and Christians read these lines as being about God's faithfulness.
Someone with no faith in God can still borrow the move underneath: recall one thing that was kind today. Fourth, why small.
This is not a silver lining. Last week, the line was growth isn't required, and that still stands.
A small mercy doesn't explain the bad day or make it worth it. It doesn't cancel the test results. It just sits next to them: a warm roll, a held door, a text from a friend.
The poet in Lamentations doesn't stop lamenting after this verse. The book goes on grieving. He has simply found one thing to hold while it does.

how: Jewish and Christian readers return to Lamentations 3:22–23, 'they are new every morning', on hard days, and some people keep a nightly habit of naming one good thing from the day.

games.q: you're the poet in Lamentations. the city is in ruins and you've forgotten what good feels like. what comes next in the poem?
o: recall something else that is also true.
games.why: "this I recall to my mind, therefore have I hope." he doesn't deny the ruins; he turns his attention to mercies new every morning.

practice: Let today play back for a moment, hard parts included, without arguing with them. Then look for one small mercy, small enough to miss: a kind word, hot water, a song in a shop, a minute when nothing hurt, and stay with it.
If you pray, you can give thanks in your own words, or with the line from Lamentations, they are new every morning, then breathe beside it.

wordCard.voice: Hesed, the Hebrew word behind mercies in Lamentations: God's mercies, new every morning, recalled on purpose inside the ruin. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew, from Lamentations 3:22, where the King James 'mercies' translates this word in the plural.

carryVoice: Your line: they are new every morning. A mercy doesn't have to be big to be real. Day seven hundred forty-four, done.
